newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - Weak while overhang persists.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - Weak while overhang persists.

text.p: The North Sea physical crude market was likely to see differentials weaken further this week with an overhang of unsold December cargoes weighing the market down, dealers said.

Physical Brent was seen due to fall another 10 cents from Friday's valuation of 15 cents discount to January paper. This week is likely to see the first January barrels trade at 15-20 cent discount to January paper, a further trader said.
"There are some half a dozen to 10 other cargoes not yet sold. There is a bit of an end year overhang," he said.
He and others believed the overhang would shift as refiners looked to cover early January requirements ahead of the Christmas holidays with prices low enough to tempt them.
"There is a lot of pressure on Brent. It depends on how the new programmes get in and how they are viewed. We may see a lot of activity on January barrels," a broker said.
Most January North Sea loading programmes for the largest fields were released last week, showing roughly unchanged prodution from December.
December Forties, Oseberg and Statfjord were among grades still waiting for homes.
Colder weather forecast for Europe this week was seen supportive of gas oil, which traders said should keep margins positive after the sharp falls in crude's outright value.
Traders saw the transatlantic arbitrage, though still tight, creaking open to let some West African and North Sea grades travel out of the region and take some of the pressure off.
The LLS/Dated Brent spread opened by $1 per barrel late last week, ending the week at $2.30 per barrel.
Traders reported brisk activity in West African grades with early January cargoes already snapped up by European and Far Eastern customers and prices firming, particularly for Cabinda.
In the Mediterranean, the return of Iraqi crude oil exports was the main talk with potential buyers of Russian Urals discouraged by recent high differentials holding back.
Recent tightness in supply was easing with the first tanker loading Iraqi crude oil from Ceyhan in Turkey on Monday.
Med traders saw prompt Urals cargoes under pressure once berth number one at Novorossiisk reopens at the end of the two-week maintenance period which started last Monday.
"There is enough Urals around to meet demand and there is a lot more supply than there is demand at the moment," a sour trader for an oil major said.
"The Iraqi threat is looming and the barrels will soon appear. We have got closer than ever before on that."
Iraq's Kirkuk crude has been priced at a discount of $1.55 a barrel below Dated Brent, which makes it very competitive with Urals at current levels, traders say.
"Certainly it will displace Urals for sure. When berth number one comes back, there's going to be a lot around and it will have an effect on the market," the trader said.
